title: The Fuzzy Invitation Supper
markdown:
Hazel the squirrel felt it first in her tail: not a map, a twitch. She lived in a room that smelled of playdough and books, a cosy cage for a spirit that preferred wind. Beside her, Teddy Walnut contemplated the shelf with button eyes that had filed a silent request for elsewhere.

Every day the window did its work. Sun on the floor. The ancient oak outside told distant-land stories in a language of leaves. They listened. Their world, however, was tied to Leo’s sleep. When his lids fluttered, adventures had to pretend they had never left the carpet.

Until one night Leo slept as if he meant it. The moon was a sliver. A scroll no bigger than a dandelion-puff came through the open window, shut with a swirl of ink and a bit of fluff. Hazel’s whiskers went to work.

“Teddy. An invitation. Supper in the Hazel Copse.”

Teddy blinked. “We sent no invitations.”

She was already at the shelf’s edge, tail a banner. “That is what makes it interesting.”

Because of that, the unauthorised expedition began: paws, stuffing, the cool damp of honeysuckle. The lawn under moonlight was a wilderness if you were the right height. They met Toad Giles on an ancient stone.

“A fine evening,” Hazel tried.

The toad’s voice was pebbles. “You are a squirrel.”

“We are on our way to supper.”

He furrowed. “A supposition. Attendance requires an invitation. I have received none. The premise is flawed.”

Some creatures were logic with damp skin. They went around him. The wind rustled them onward. The hazel copse made a tangle of moon-branches. Beneath a mossy log: a feast. Dewdrop jelly glistened. Blackberries. Acorn pastries that crunched when the breeze so much as thought about them. Woodland faces, surprised, already sampling.

“So glad you could make it,” squeaked a field mouse, offering pastry. “We were about to start.”

Because of that they sat, unexpected guests who had been expected after all. The policy, it emerged, was Everyone Who Feels Invited. The mouse had found a scrap and assumed neighbours. Hazel named it the most spontaneous supper on record. Teddy occupied the jelly. “Quite pleasingly damp.”

The hiccup arrived on webbed feet. Toad Giles, needing to resolve his paradox, stood at the clearing’s edge. “I am here to observe the supposition of attendance.”

Silence, then a portly badger’s laugh. “You came because you supposed you might be invited.”

The copse went up like a kettle. Even Giles managed a perplexed chuckle. The misunderstanding sat down and became the evening’s best dish.

Until finally dawn softened. Hazel nudged Teddy. “Quite an adventure.”

“The finest dewdrop jelly,” he said, “is enjoyed when the invitation is a little fuzzy.”

They did not need to name the bond. It had eaten supper with them.

Ever since then Leo’s room kept a faint extra shimmer, as if fluff-ink had a half-life. Hazel’s tail still twitched, but toward the next maybe-invitation, and the oak went on whispering, and nobody in the copse could remember who had posted the original scroll, which was, if you thought about it, the point.
characters: Hazel (auburn squirrel whose tail twitches for adventure), Teddy Walnut (a bear of quiet contemplation)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
